question: The European Court of Auditors’ annual report on EU joint undertakings for the 2024 financial year reveals significant delays in the implementation of operational budgets, particularly in strategic sectors such as semiconductors, supercomputing, hydrogen and cybersecurity.

It also emphasises that ‘fewer than half’ of the observations and shortcomings reported in previous years have been addressed, and that a number of joint undertakings make ‘disproportionate use of external service providers’, hindering the retention of skills in the EU. 1.

Given these circumstances, does the Commission acknowledge that the proliferation of structures and programmes has not enabled the EU to achieve real industrial sovereignty and that the EU risks replacing actual power with bureaucracy?

Will it strengthen internal skills management and budget transparency, curb the fragmentation of partnerships and agencies, and ensure that European investments generate concrete industrial capacities rather than additional administrative structures?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (24.2.2026) Joint Undertakings (JU) align research and innovation (R&I) investments across EU, national and regional level, and between industry and academia, enabling flexible responses to EU challenges and avoiding fragmentation and providing more co-steering role to the industry.

The Horizon Europe Interim Evaluation Report1 highlights JU’s role in advancing EU leadership in semiconductors, health technologies and clean hydrogen, reinforcing value chains and securing a competitive edge for EU companies. Under Pillar II, JUs show also the highest direct leverage factor (0.8).

In 2024, Chips JU2, European High Performance Computing JU3 and Clean Aviation JU4 faced low operational budget implementation due to respectively delays in procurement agreements, redeployment of resources to the new AI factories pillar and slow implementation of 2023 projects.

Intensive use of external service providers is specific to fusion for energy5 and it is due to the purpose of the JU to deliver the Euratom contribution to the International Thermonuclear Experimental Reactor. In table 2.4, the European Court of Auditors (ECA) report outlines the actions undertaken in this regard.

Moreover, the Commission is closely monitoring the past observations not yet addressed by the JUs towards their implementation by the target date set out by the ECA. The Horizon Europe 2028-20346 and the European Competitiveness Fund proposals of the Commission7 seek to continue to streamline the partnership portfolio, using Treaty-based instruments where their impact is highest.

Budget transparency will be ensured through rigorous monitoring, reporting and audits in line with the applicable rules. Simplification measures (i.e. lump sum funding, personnel unit costs) are underway to reduce administrative burden and increase focus on project results.
